description: Orbitalis is a student led team passionate about space, science, and technology. We combine software development, scientific curiosity, and creative problem-solving to turn NASA data into meaningful, interactive experiences. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to build an innovative solution that connects Earth-based environments with the future of lunar and Martian exploration.
summary:
Orbitalis CrewCare is an astronaut health monitoring and decision-support prototype designed to support crew well-being during long-duration space missions. Developed by Team Orbitalis, the system brings together astronaut health profiles, baseline tracking, wearable sensor inputs, simulated physiological and environmental data, and intelligent assessment engines to identify potential health and well-being concerns.

The platform evaluates changes in individual health indicators, considers environmental conditions, and provides structured alerts and response recommendations to support informed crew-health decisions. It also incorporates scientific research and publicly available NASA biomedical datasets to strengthen its knowledge base.

As astronauts travel farther from Earth, continuous health awareness and timely decision support become increasingly important, especially when immediate medical assistance is limited. CrewCare aims to help bridge this gap through an integrated, adaptable digital tool that supports safer and more informed human space exploration.
details:
Project Details – Orbitalis CrewCare

Orbitalis CrewCare is an integrated astronaut health monitoring and decision-support prototype designed to support crew health and well-being during long-duration space missions.

How It Works

The system combines individual astronaut health profiles, personal baseline tracking, wearable sensor inputs, physiological measurements, and environmental information to build an overview of crew health.

Its assessment engines evaluate incoming data, compare measurements against individual baselines and configured assessment criteria, and identify potential concerns. The platform then presents health assessments, alerts, and structured response recommendations through a unified dashboard.

CrewCare also incorporates a scientific knowledge base informed by publicly available biomedical research and NASA datasets, including the OSD-575 cardiovascular dataset. This research helps provide context for understanding health-related changes during spaceflight.

The current prototype uses simulated data for several physiological and environmental measurements, alongside a wearable-data simulation system and compatible heart-rate input functionality. It is a decision-support prototype, not a clinically validated diagnostic system.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars will place astronauts in environments where immediate medical assistance from Earth may be difficult or delayed. Changes in cardiovascular health, physical condition, psychological well-being, and environmental exposure can affect mission safety and performance.

CrewCare aims to support earlier awareness of potential health concerns, improve access to organized crew-health information, and help astronauts and mission support teams make more informed decisions. Its modular design could also support future integration with additional sensors, research datasets, and mission-health systems.

Technologies and Tools

The project was developed using JavaScript and React, with Vite as the development and build tool. Its frontend uses HTML and CSS, while modular JavaScript assessment engines handle baseline tracking, data validation, physiological assessment, environmental assessment, well-being assessment, and response recommendations.

The prototype also incorporates simulated wearable sensor inputs, a Bluetooth heart-rate integration module, and publicly available NASA biomedical research data. Git and GitHub were used for source-code management and public project hosting.

Creativity and Innovation

CrewCare brings multiple aspects of astronaut health into one integrated platform rather than treating each measurement as an isolated value. Its combination of personal baseline tracking, modular assessment engines, environmental context, scientific research, and structured response recommendations creates a flexible approach to astronaut health decision support.

The system is designed to be expandable as new sensors, research findings, and mission requirements become available.

Factors Considered

Our team considered the challenges of limited medical access during deep-space missions, individual differences in astronaut health, the importance of reliable data, environmental influences, and the need for understandable information during time-sensitive situations.

We also considered the limitations of a prototype developed within a hackathon. Simulated measurements are clearly distinguished from actual sensor inputs, and the system is intended to support—not replace—professional medical judgment.
